intro: You already link words and keep the small words weak. Now meet real, fast English: sounds that disappear (last night → 'las night'), sounds that change (ten people → 'tem people'), small words that shrink to almost nothing, and gonna, wanna and gotta. The main goal is to understand fast speech, and to know which forms are fine to say but never to write.
teachingNotes: Builds on a2-pron-stress-linking (content vs function words, consonant → vowel linking: tur-noff), a2-pron-ed-weak-forms (the weak 'uh' sound = the e of Indonesian emas; weak was/can/to/of) and b1-pron-rhythm-intonation (stress-timed rhythm, weak 'tuh', 'fuh', 'kuhn'). Recap in a line, don't re-teach. New here: elision, assimilation, weak forms at full speed (and → 'n', of → 'uh' as in 'a cuppa tea' / 'a lotta', them → 'em') and gonna/wanna/gotta. The main skill is LISTENING: hearing fast speech and 'undoing' the changes in your head (catch the strong words, rebuild the small ones, undo the sound changes, use context). For speaking, aim at natural linking and weak forms; never force extreme reductions: clear full forms are always acceptable.

Elision (a sound disappears): a t or d between two consonant sounds often drops: next door 'nex door', last night 'las night', handbag 'hanbag', must be 'mus be', an old friend 'an ol friend', left my 'lef my'. Before a vowel it stays and links instead (just a minute 'jus-ta minute', first of all 'firs-tof all', hold on 'hol-don'). The -ed ending can disappear too (worked late ≈ 'work late'): tell learners to use time words to hear the tense. Assimilation (a sound changes towards the next one): n → m before p, b, m (ten people 'tem people', in Bandung 'im Bandung'); d → b and t → p before p, b, m (good boy 'goob boy', that man 'thap man'); t + you → 'ch' like Indonesian c in cari (don't you 'doncha', meet you 'meecha'); d + you → 'j' like Indonesian j in jalan (did you 'didja', would you 'wouldja', could you 'couldja'). Indonesian link: meN- changes with the next sound (membeli, mendengar, menggambar). Use everyday respellings, never bare IPA, no terms like 'yod coalescence'. These are tendencies of relaxed speech, not rules: careful speakers keep the sounds.

Weak forms at full speed: to 'tuh', for 'fuh' (American 'fer'), and → 'n' (fish 'n' chips), can 'kn' (can't is always strong), of → 'uh' (a cuppa tea, a lotta people), them → 'em' (sounds like the letter M). Strong forms: at the end of a sentence (Who's it for?), in short answers (Yes, we can.), in negatives. Node common error: every word said fully and separately, 'I – am – going – to – go'; right: linked with weak forms, 'I'm GOing tuh GO'. Indonesian trap: Indonesian is said as written, syllable by syllable, so learners wait for each word as a separate unit and get lost; teach them to catch the strong words first and rebuild the small ones from grammar. You may mention him → 'im' and her → 'er' if asked, but don't drill them.

gonna = going to + a verb (future plans) only; going to a PLACE never becomes gonna (I'm going to the office, not 'gonna the office'). wanna = want to after I/you/we/they; she wants to never becomes wanna. (wanna can also be 'want a': mention only if asked.) gotta = have got to / has got to (= have to); in very casual speech the have disappears ('I gotta go'). Register: saying going to quickly so it sounds close to 'gonna' is normal even at work; WRITING gonna/wanna/gotta is only for chats with friends: never in emails, reports, essays, CVs, or messages to clients, lecturers or managers. Node common errors: not recognising gonna as going to; 'I wanna ask' in a work email (right: I would like to ask). Indonesian comparison: gimana, nggak, udah, makasih are fine on WhatsApp with friends, not in a letter to a lecturer.

Audio limits: every recording is read once by one voice, naturally, with natural but not extreme connected speech. Listen texts and read-aloud tiles are always written in full standard spelling (never gonna/wanna/gotta), and listening questions ask which full words were said or which small word was heard. Don't promise that the audio shows each change clearly: describe it and ask the learner to say it slowly, then fast. British vs American: Americans often turn a t between vowels into a quick soft d ('a lodda', 'godda'); British speakers often swallow it. Both are common; recognise, don't drill.

Grammar scope: A0–B1 grammar (present and past tenses, present perfect, going to, will, have to / have got to, can/could/would for requests, first and second conditionals). No third conditional, wish or past modals, so no 'shoulda/woulda/coulda'. Don't teach intrusion (the small r/w/y sounds), glottal stops or t-flapping as targets, and don't use phonetic symbols.

keyPoints.title: Sounds disappear and change
keyPoints.explanation: In fast speech a t or d between two consonant sounds often disappears (elision): next door → 'nex door', last night → 'las night', handbag → 'hanbag'. Before a vowel it stays and links instead: just a minute → 'jus-ta minute'. Other sounds change to get ready for the next one (assimilation): n → m before p, b, m (ten people → 'tem people'); t + you → 'ch' and d + you → 'j' (don't you → 'doncha', would you → 'wouldja'). When you listen, undo the change in your head.

examples.id: Tetanggaku tinggal di sebelah rumah. ('nex door': t-nya hilang)

examples.en: There were ten people in the meeting.
examples.id: Ada sepuluh orang di rapat itu. ('tem people': n jadi m)

id.title: Bunyi yang hilang dan berubah
id.explanation: Dalam ucapan cepat, t atau d yang terjepit di antara dua bunyi konsonan sering hilang (elision): next door → 'nex door', last night → 'las night', handbag → 'hanbag'. Sebelum bunyi vokal, t-nya tetap ada dan menyambung: just a minute → 'jus-ta minute'. Bunyi lain berubah supaya siap untuk bunyi berikutnya (assimilation): n → m sebelum p, b, m (ten people → 'tem people'); t + you → 'ch' dan d + you → 'j' (don't you → 'doncha', would you → 'wouldja'). Saat mendengarkan, kembalikan perubahan itu di kepalamu.

keyPoints.title: Small words shrink in fast speech
keyPoints.explanation: In the middle of a fast sentence the small words become tiny: to → 'tuh', for → 'fuh', and → just 'n', can → 'kn', of → 'uh', them → 'em'. Don't say every word fully and separately ('I – am – going – to – go'); link them and keep them weak. They are strong at the end of a sentence, in short answers and in negatives (Yes, we can. / I can't.). For listening: catch the strong words first, then rebuild the small ones.

examples.en: Can you get some bread and milk for me?
examples.id: Bisa belikan roti dan susu untukku? ('kn yuh GET sum BREAD n MILK fuh me')

examples.en: Tell them I'm on my way.
examples.id: Bilang ke mereka aku lagi di jalan. ('TELL em')

id.title: Kata-kata kecil menyusut dalam ucapan cepat
id.explanation: Di tengah kalimat yang cepat, kata-kata kecil jadi sangat pendek: to → 'te', for → 'fe', and → cuma 'n', can → 'kn', of → 'e', them → 'em' (e di sini = e lemah seperti di emas). Jangan ucapkan setiap kata dengan penuh dan terpisah ('I – am – going – to – go'); sambungkan dan buat lemah. Kata-kata itu kuat di akhir kalimat, di jawaban pendek dan di bentuk negatif (Yes, we can. / I can't.). Saat mendengarkan: tangkap dulu kata-kata kuatnya, lalu susun kembali kata-kata kecilnya.

keyPoints.title: gonna, wanna, gotta: hear them, don't write them
keyPoints.explanation: gonna = going to + a verb, wanna = want to, gotta = have got to (= have to). You'll hear them in films, songs and casual talk. A place is never gonna (I'm going to the office), and she wants to is never wanna. They're informal: fine to hear and to say with friends, but never write them in emails, reports or essays: I would like to ask (not I wanna ask).

examples.id: Kita bakal telat. (cepat: 'we're gonna be late')

examples.en: I would like to know more about the course.
examples.id: Saya ingin tahu lebih banyak tentang kursusnya. (di email: bukan 'I wanna know')

id.title: gonna, wanna, gotta: kenali saat didengar, jangan ditulis
id.explanation: gonna = going to + kata kerja, wanna = want to, gotta = have got to (= have to, harus). Kamu akan mendengarnya di film, lagu dan obrolan santai. Tempat tidak pernah jadi gonna (I'm going to the office), dan she wants to tidak pernah jadi wanna. Bentuk ini informal: boleh didengar dan diucapkan dengan teman, tapi jangan pernah ditulis di email, laporan atau esai: I would like to ask (bukan I wanna ask).

guidedPractice.prompt: Budi says quickly: 'We stayed at the office until late las' night.' Write the word he said before 'night', in full.
guidedPractice.hint: The t is stuck between s and n, two consonant sounds, so it disappears in fast speech: 'las night' = last night.

guidedPractice.prompt: Sari says quickly: 'I bought tem pens.' How many pens did she buy? Write the number.
guidedPractice.hint: n becomes m before p, b or m, because the lips are already closing for the p: 'tem pens' = ten pens.

guidedPractice.prompt: At a warung, Rina asks: 'Salt 'n' pepper?' What is 'n'? Write the full word.
guidedPractice.hint: In fast speech and often shrinks to just 'n' between two things: fish 'n' chips, salt 'n' pepper.

guidedPractice.prompt: Write the sentence with the full words: Do you wanna join us for lunch?
expected: do you want to join us for lunch
guidedPractice.hint: wanna = want to. Write the two full words.

independentPractice.prompt: Write the full words: 'Didja see the news this morning?'
expected: did you see the news this morning
independentPractice.hint: d + you sounds like 'ja', so 'didja' = did you.

independentPractice.prompt: In the short answer 'Yes, I can.', is 'can' weak ('kn') or strong? Write weak or strong.
independentPractice.hint: Small words are strong at the end of a sentence and in short answers.

independentPractice.prompt: Correct the mistake: Budi is gonna the gym after work.
expected: budi is going to the gym after work
budi's going to the gym after work
budis going to the gym after work
independentPractice.hint: Here going to means moving to a place (the gym), not going to + a verb, so it never becomes gonna.

assessment.prompt: In a meeting, your manager says: 'I'm gonna send the new prices to the client tomorrow.' Write the same sentence with the full words, as you would write it in an email.
acceptableAnswers: i'm going to send the new prices to the client tomorrow
i am going to send the new prices to the client tomorrow
im going to send the new prices to the client tomorrow
assessment.rubric: Correct: I'm going to / I am going to send the new prices to the client tomorrow (gonna = going to + a verb). 'I will send…' or 'I'll send…' = 60 (fine in an email, but the full form of gonna is going to). 'I'm going send…' (to missing) = 40. Keeping gonna = 0.

assessment.prompt: Sari says about her colleague: 'She's gotta pick up her kids at five.' Write the sentence with the full words.
acceptableAnswers: she's got to pick up her kids at five
she has got to pick up her kids at five
shes got to pick up her kids at five
she has to pick up her kids at five
she's got to pick her kids up at five
she has got to pick her kids up at five
she has to pick her kids up at five
she's got to pick up her kids at 5
she has got to pick up her kids at 5
she has to pick up her kids at 5
assessment.rubric: Correct: She's got to / She has got to pick up her kids at five (gotta = got to; 's here = has). 'She has to pick up…' = 100 (same meaning, standard English). 'She is got to…' = 30 ('s is has here, not is). 'She got to pick up…' = 50 (has is missing, and it can mean 'had the chance to'). Keeping gotta = 0.

assessment.prompt: In fast speech, 'next door' often sounds like 'nex door'. Which sound disappears? Write the letter.
acceptableAnswers: t
the t
t sound
the t sound
assessment.rubric: Correct: t (it's stuck between the s sound at the end of 'nex' and the d of door, two consonant sounds, so it drops). 'x' = 0 (the x, said 'ks', is still there: 'nex'). 'd' = 0 (the d of door is the first sound of the next word and stays).

assessment.prompt: At the office, Rina asks Budi quickly: 'Couldja check this email for me?' Which two words does 'couldja' stand for? Write them.
acceptableAnswers: could you
assessment.rubric: Correct: could you (d + you blends into 'ja', like did you → 'didja' and would you → 'wouldja'). 'could ya' = 50 (still the fast form). 'could' alone = 40. 'can you' = 30 (a request with the same meaning, but not the words she said).

assessment.prompt: Budi says quickly: 'I've got the concert tickets. I'll send 'em to you tonight.' Which word does 'em stand for? Write the full word.
acceptableAnswers: them
assessment.rubric: Correct: them ('em is the weak form of them in fast speech; here them = the tickets). 'it' = 30 (tickets is plural). 'him' = 0 (its fast form is 'im', and it means a man, not the tickets).

assessment.prompt: Listen. Write the small word you hear between 'leave' and 'the airport'.
assessment.listen: We need to leave for the airport at six.
acceptableAnswers: for
assessment.rubric: Correct: for (said weak and quick, 'fuh': leave for a place = go to it). 'to' = 30 ('leave to the airport' isn't English; to is the small word before leave). 'four' = 0 (a number makes no sense here).

assessment.prompt: Rina is writing an email to a supplier. Which sentence should she use? Write A, B or C. A: I wanna ask about the price. B: I would like to ask about the price. C: I gotta ask about the price.
acceptableAnswers: b
b i would like to ask about the price
i would like to ask about the price
assessment.rubric: Correct: B (would like to is polite and right for an email). A = 0 (wanna is informal speech: the common error 'I wanna ask' in a work email). C = 0 (gotta is informal speech, and it means 'have to', not a polite request).

blocks.text:
Quick recap: you already **link** a consonant to a vowel (*turn off* → 'tur-noff'), make small words **weak** ('tuh', 'kn') and keep the English **beat**. In fast, relaxed speech English goes one step further: some sounds **disappear** and some **change**. This is called **connected speech**. It's the main reason fast English is hard to hear: the words you know don't sound like the words in your dictionary.

(A **consonant** sound is a 'huruf mati' sound like t, d, s, n, b. A **vowel** sound is a 'huruf hidup' sound like a, e, i, o, u.)

**Elision** = a sound disappears. The most common case: a **t** or **d** stuck **between two consonant sounds** is often dropped, because three consonants in a row are hard to say quickly:
- *next door* → 'nex door' (the t is stuck between the s sound of x and the d)
- *last night* → 'las night'
- *handbag* → 'hanbag'
- *must be* → 'mus be'
- *an old friend* → 'an ol friend'

**What seems to break the rule:** *just a minute* keeps its t: 'jus-ta minute'. Why? The next word starts with a **vowel** sound, so the t isn't stuck between consonants: it **links** to the vowel, as you learnt before. The same with *first of all* → 'firs-tof all' and *hold on* → 'hol-don'.

**Remember:** this happens in relaxed, fast speech. In careful speech (a presentation, a phone number, a name) people keep the t and d. You don't *have* to drop them yourself; the big win is **hearing** them.

id.text:
Ulasan singkat: kamu sudah bisa **menyambung** konsonan ke vokal (*turn off* → 'tur-noff'), membuat kata-kata kecil **lemah** ('te', 'kn') dan menjaga **ketukan** bahasa Inggris. Dalam ucapan yang cepat dan santai, bahasa Inggris melangkah lebih jauh: sebagian bunyi **hilang** dan sebagian **berubah**. Ini disebut **connected speech** (ucapan yang menyambung). Inilah alasan utama bahasa Inggris yang cepat susah didengar: kata-kata yang kamu tahu tidak terdengar seperti di kamus.

(Bunyi **konsonan** = bunyi 'huruf mati' seperti t, d, s, n, b. Bunyi **vokal** = bunyi 'huruf hidup' seperti a, e, i, o, u.)

**Elision** = sebuah bunyi hilang. Yang paling sering: **t** atau **d** yang **terjepit di antara dua bunyi konsonan** sering tidak diucapkan, karena tiga konsonan berturut-turut susah diucapkan dengan cepat:
- *next door* → 'nex door' (t-nya terjepit di antara bunyi s dari x dan d)
- *last night* → 'las night'
- *handbag* → 'hanbag'
- *must be* → 'mus be'
- *an old friend* → 'an ol friend'

**Yang kelihatannya melanggar aturan:** *just a minute* tetap punya t: 'jus-ta minute'. Kenapa? Kata berikutnya mulai dengan bunyi **vokal**, jadi t-nya tidak terjepit di antara konsonan: t-nya **menyambung** ke vokal, seperti yang sudah kamu pelajari. Sama dengan *first of all* → 'firs-tof all' dan *hold on* → 'hol-don'.

**Ingat:** ini terjadi dalam ucapan yang santai dan cepat. Dalam ucapan yang hati-hati (presentasi, nomor telepon, nama) orang tetap mengucapkan t dan d. Kamu tidak *harus* menghilangkannya sendiri; yang paling penting adalah bisa **mendengarnya**.

rows.note: 'I lef my hanbag': two sounds disappear

id.note: 'I lef my hanbag': dua bunyi hilang

rows.note: 'we work late las night': even the -ed can disappear, so listen for the time words

id.note: 'we work late las night': -ed pun bisa hilang, jadi dengarkan kata-kata waktunya

rows.note: before a vowel the t stays and links: 'jus-ta minute'

blocks.text: The Indonesian trap: we expect to hear every letter we see in the written word, so 'las night' sounds like a word we don't know. When you can't find a word, ask yourself: could a t or d be missing? And if a past -ed seems to vanish (*worked late* → 'work late'), let the time words (*yesterday, last night*) tell you it's the past.

id.text: Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia: kita berharap mendengar setiap huruf yang kita lihat di tulisan, jadi 'las night' terdengar seperti kata yang tidak kita kenal. Kalau kamu tidak menemukan katanya, tanya dirimu: mungkinkah ada t atau d yang hilang? Dan kalau -ed bentuk lampau seperti lenyap (*worked late* → 'work late'), biarkan kata-kata waktunya (*yesterday, last night*) memberitahumu bahwa itu masa lalu.

blocks.prompt: In fast speech, which phrase usually loses its d?
blocks.explain: In *an old friend* the d is stuck between l and f, two consonant sounds, so it often drops: 'an ol friend'. In *old age* and *hold on* the next word starts with a vowel sound, so the d links instead: 'ol-dage', 'hol-don'.

id.prompt: Dalam ucapan cepat, frasa mana yang biasanya kehilangan d-nya?
id.explain: Di *an old friend* d-nya terjepit di antara l dan f, dua bunyi konsonan, jadi sering hilang: 'an ol friend'. Di *old age* dan *hold on* kata berikutnya mulai dengan bunyi vokal, jadi d-nya justru menyambung: 'ol-dage', 'hol-don'.

blocks.text:
**Assimilation** = a sound **changes** to become more like the next sound. Your mouth is already getting ready for the next word, so it takes a shortcut.
- **n → m** before p, b or m (the sounds you make with closed lips): *ten people* → 'tem people', *in Bandung* → 'im Bandung', *a green bag* → 'a greem bag'.
- **d → b** and **t → p** before p, b or m: *a good boy* → 'a goob boy', *that man* → 'thap man'.
- **t + you → 'ch'** (like the c in Indonesian *cari*): *don't you* → 'doncha', *meet you* → 'meecha', *got you* → 'gotcha'.
- **d + you → 'j'** (like the j in *jalan*): *did you* → 'didja', *would you* → 'wouldja', *need you* → 'needja'.

Try it: say *ten people* slowly, then fast. Your lips close for the p already during the n, so it comes out as m.

For listening, **undo the change**: 'tem' before a p is probably *ten*; 'cha' or 'ja' after a verb or a helper like *did* or *would* is probably *you*.

id.text:
**Assimilation** = sebuah bunyi **berubah** supaya lebih mirip bunyi berikutnya. Mulutmu sudah bersiap untuk kata berikutnya, jadi mengambil jalan pintas.
- **n → m** sebelum p, b atau m (bunyi yang dibuat dengan bibir tertutup): *ten people* → 'tem people', *in Bandung* → 'im Bandung', *a green bag* → 'a greem bag'.
- **d → b** dan **t → p** sebelum p, b atau m: *a good boy* → 'a goob boy', *that man* → 'thap man'.
- **t + you → 'ch'** (seperti c di kata *cari*): *don't you* → 'doncha', *meet you* → 'meecha', *got you* → 'gotcha'.
- **d + you → 'j'** (seperti j di kata *jalan*): *did you* → 'didja', *would you* → 'wouldja', *need you* → 'needja'.

Coba: ucapkan *ten people* pelan-pelan, lalu cepat. Bibirmu sudah menutup untuk p sewaktu mengucapkan n, jadi yang keluar adalah m.

Saat mendengarkan, **kembalikan perubahannya**: 'tem' sebelum p kemungkinan besar *ten*; 'cha' atau 'ja' setelah kata kerja atau kata bantu seperti *did* atau *would* kemungkinan besar *you*.

rows.en: There were ten people in the room.
rows.id: Ada sepuluh orang di ruangan itu.

blocks.text: You already know this from Indonesian! The prefix me- changes with the next sound: **mem**beli (before b), **men**dengar (before d), **meng**gambar (before g). English *ten people* → 'tem people' is the same idea: the n becomes m because the lips are getting ready for p.

id.text: Sebenarnya kamu sudah kenal ini dari bahasa Indonesia! Awalan me- berubah mengikuti bunyi berikutnya: **mem**beli (sebelum b), **men**dengar (sebelum d), **meng**gambar (sebelum g). Bahasa Inggris *ten people* → 'tem people' idenya sama: n berubah jadi m karena bibir sudah bersiap untuk p.

blocks.prompt: You hear: 'I've lived im Bekasi for five years.' What is 'im'?
blocks.explain: It's **in**: n becomes m before the b of Bekasi, so *in Bekasi* sounds like 'im Bekasi'. *lived him Bekasi* and *lived I'm Bekasi* make no sense.

id.prompt: Kamu mendengar: 'I've lived im Bekasi for five years.' Apa 'im' itu?
id.explain: Itu **in**: n berubah jadi m sebelum b di Bekasi, jadi *in Bekasi* terdengar seperti 'im Bekasi'. *lived him Bekasi* dan *lived I'm Bekasi* tidak masuk akal.

blocks.text:
You know that small words are **weak** in the middle of a sentence: *to* → 'tuh', *can* → 'kn', *of* → 'uhv'. ('uh' = the short, lazy e of Indonesian *emas*.) In fast speech they shrink even more, sometimes to one sound:
- **to** → 'tuh': *I need to leave* → 'ai NEED tuh LEAVE'
- **for** → 'fuh' (British) or 'fer' (American): *a present for Rina* → 'uh PRE-sent fuh RI-na'
- **and** → just **'n'**: *fish and chips* → 'fish 'n' chips', *Sari and Budi* → 'SA-ri n BU-di'
- **can** → 'kn': *We can meet at ten* → 'we kn MEET at TEN'
- **of** → just 'uh': *a cup of tea* → 'a cuppa tea', *a lot of people* → 'a lotta people'
- **them** → **'em'**: *Call them now* → 'CALL em NOW' (it sounds like the letter M!)

**The common mistake** is saying every word fully and separately: 'I – am – going – to – go'. Natural English links the words and keeps the small ones weak: 'I'm GO-ing tuh GO'.

**When are they strong?** At the end of a sentence (*Who's it **for**?*), in short answers (*Yes, we **can**.*), and in negatives (*can't* is always strong).

id.text:
Kamu sudah tahu bahwa kata-kata kecil itu **lemah** di tengah kalimat: *to* → 'te', *can* → 'kn', *of* → 'ev'. (e di sini = e pendek dan lemah seperti di *emas*.) Dalam ucapan cepat kata-kata itu menyusut lagi, kadang tinggal satu bunyi:
- **to** → 'te': *I need to leave* → 'ai NEED te LEAVE'
- **for** → 'fe' (British) atau 'fer' (Amerika): *a present for Rina* → 'e PRE-sent fe RI-na'
- **and** → cuma **'n'**: *fish and chips* → 'fish 'n' chips', *Sari and Budi* → 'SA-ri n BU-di'
- **can** → 'kn': *We can meet at ten* → 'we kn MEET at TEN'
- **of** → cuma 'e': *a cup of tea* → 'a cuppa tea', *a lot of people* → 'a lotta people'
- **them** → **'em'**: *Call them now* → 'CALL em NOW' (bunyinya seperti huruf M!)

**Kesalahan yang sering terjadi** adalah mengucapkan setiap kata dengan penuh dan terpisah: 'I – am – going – to – go'. Bahasa Inggris yang alami menyambung kata-katanya dan membuat kata-kata kecil tetap lemah: 'I'm GO-ing te GO'.

**Kapan kata-kata itu kuat?** Di akhir kalimat (*Who's it **for**?*), di jawaban pendek (*Yes, we **can**.*), dan di bentuk negatif (*can't* selalu kuat).

Tell them I'm on my way.

blocks.text: The Indonesian trap: Indonesian is said as it's written, syllable by syllable, so we wait to hear every word clearly. In English the small words are almost hidden. Listen for the **strong** words first (who, what, where, when), then rebuild the small words from grammar: 'NEED … LEAVE' must be *need to leave*. Missed a small word? Don't stop: keep listening.

id.text: Jebakan untuk orang Indonesia: bahasa Indonesia diucapkan seperti tulisannya, suku kata demi suku kata, jadi kita menunggu setiap kata terdengar jelas. Dalam bahasa Inggris kata-kata kecil hampir tersembunyi. Dengarkan dulu kata-kata yang **kuat** (siapa, apa, di mana, kapan), lalu susun kembali kata-kata kecilnya dari tata bahasa: 'NEED … LEAVE' pasti *need to leave*. Ada kata kecil yang terlewat? Jangan berhenti: terus dengarkan.

blocks.prompt: You hear: 'I'd like a cuppa coffee.' Which word is the 'a' after 'cup' really?
blocks.explain: It's **of**: *a cup of coffee*. In fast speech *of* shrinks to a quick 'uh' and joins the word before it: 'cuppa'. *a cup a coffee* or *a cup the coffee* aren't English.

id.prompt: Kamu mendengar: 'I'd like a cuppa coffee.' Kata apa sebenarnya 'a' setelah 'cup'?
id.explain: Itu **of**: *a cup of coffee*. Dalam ucapan cepat *of* menyusut jadi 'e' yang cepat dan menempel ke kata sebelumnya: 'cuppa'. *a cup a coffee* atau *a cup the coffee* bukan bahasa Inggris.

material.title: gonna, wanna, gotta: hear them, don't write them

blocks.text:
Three very common fast-speech forms. You'll hear them all the time in films, songs, YouTube videos and casual talk:
- **gonna** = **going to** + a verb (plans for the future): *I'm going to call you* → 'I'm gonna call you'.
- **wanna** = **want to**: *Do you want to come?* → 'Do you wanna come?'
- **gotta** = **have got to** / **has got to** (= have to, *harus*): *I've got to go* → 'I've gotta go', or just 'I gotta go'.

**Two things that seem to break the rule:**
- *gonna* is only for **going to + a verb**. When *going to* means moving to a **place**, it never becomes *gonna*: *I'm going to the office* (not 'I'm gonna the office').
- *wanna* is only for **want to** after *I, you, we, they*. After *he, she, it* we say *wants to*, and that never becomes *wanna*: *She wants to rest* (not 'She wanna rest').

**They're informal.** Saying *going to* quickly, so it sounds close to 'gonna', is normal even in a meeting. But **writing** *gonna, wanna, gotta* is only for chats with friends. Never use them in emails, reports, essays, CVs or messages to clients, lecturers or your boss: write *I'm going to…*, *I want to…* or *I would like to…*, *I have to…*.

id.text:
Tiga bentuk ucapan cepat yang sangat umum. Kamu akan sering mendengarnya di film, lagu, video YouTube dan obrolan santai:
- **gonna** = **going to** + kata kerja (rencana ke depan): *I'm going to call you* → 'I'm gonna call you'.
- **wanna** = **want to**: *Do you want to come?* → 'Do you wanna come?'
- **gotta** = **have got to** / **has got to** (= have to, *harus*): *I've got to go* → 'I've gotta go', atau cuma 'I gotta go'.

**Dua hal yang kelihatannya melanggar aturan:**
- *gonna* hanya untuk **going to + kata kerja**. Kalau *going to* berarti pergi ke sebuah **tempat**, tidak pernah jadi *gonna*: *I'm going to the office* (bukan 'I'm gonna the office').
- *wanna* hanya untuk **want to** setelah *I, you, we, they*. Setelah *he, she, it* kita bilang *wants to*, dan itu tidak pernah jadi *wanna*: *She wants to rest* (bukan 'She wanna rest').

**Bentuk ini informal.** Mengucapkan *going to* dengan cepat sampai terdengar mirip 'gonna' itu biasa, bahkan di rapat. Tapi **menulis** *gonna, wanna, gotta* hanya untuk chat dengan teman. Jangan pernah memakainya di email, laporan, esai, CV atau pesan ke klien, dosen atau atasanmu: tulis *I'm going to…*, *I want to…* atau *I would like to…*, *I have to…*.

rows.en: Do you want to grab lunch?
I've got to finish this today.
rows.id: Aku harus menyelesaikan ini hari ini.

rows.en: I would like to know more about the course.
rows.id: Saya ingin tahu lebih banyak tentang kursusnya.
rows.note: in an email: not 'I wanna know'

blocks.text: It's like Indonesian *gimana, nggak, udah, makasih*: fine on WhatsApp with friends, but not in a letter to your lecturer. You'll also see *gonna* and *wanna* in song lyrics and film subtitles: learn to hear them there, but don't copy the spelling into your own writing. In American English *gotta* often sounds like 'godda'.

id.text: Mirip *gimana, nggak, udah, makasih* dalam bahasa Indonesia: boleh di WhatsApp dengan teman, tapi tidak di surat untuk dosenmu. Kamu juga akan melihat *gonna* dan *wanna* di lirik lagu dan subtitle film: belajarlah mendengarnya di sana, tapi jangan meniru ejaannya di tulisanmu sendiri. Dalam bahasa Inggris Amerika *gotta* sering terdengar seperti 'godda'.

blocks.explain: **I'm going to Surabaya tomorrow.** Here *going to* means moving to a place, so it never becomes *gonna*. *She wanna* is wrong: after *she* it's *wants to*, which never shortens to *wanna*.

id.explain: **I'm going to Surabaya tomorrow.** Di sini *going to* berarti pergi ke sebuah tempat, jadi tidak pernah jadi *gonna*. *She wanna* salah: setelah *she* yang benar *wants to*, dan itu tidak pernah disingkat jadi *wanna*.

material.title: Listening to fast English: undo the changes

blocks.text:
When fast English rushes past you, use this routine:
1. **Catch the strong words** first: names, things, main verbs, numbers. *'…SEND…RE-port…FRI-day'*
2. **Rebuild the small words** from grammar: before a verb, 'tuh' is *to*; between two things, 'n' is *and*; 'uh' between *cup, lot, piece* and a noun is *of*.
3. **Undo the sound changes**: a missing t or d ('las night' = *last night*), an m that is really n ('tem people' = *ten people*), 'cha' or 'ja' that is really *you* ('doncha' = *don't you*), and the three short forms ('gonna' = *going to*).
4. **Use the context**: time words tell you the tense even when the -ed disappears (*We worked late last night*).

id.text:
Kalau bahasa Inggris yang cepat lewat begitu saja, pakai langkah-langkah ini:
1. **Tangkap dulu kata-kata yang kuat**: nama, benda, kata kerja utama, angka. *'…SEND…RE-port…FRI-day'*
2. **Susun kembali kata-kata kecilnya** dari tata bahasa: sebelum kata kerja, 'te' adalah *to*; di antara dua benda, 'n' adalah *and*; 'e' di antara *cup, lot, piece* dan kata benda adalah *of*.
3. **Kembalikan perubahan bunyinya**: t atau d yang hilang ('las night' = *last night*), m yang sebenarnya n ('tem people' = *ten people*), 'cha' atau 'ja' yang sebenarnya *you* ('doncha' = *don't you*), dan tiga bentuk pendek ('gonna' = *going to*).
4. **Pakai konteksnya**: kata-kata waktu memberitahumu tense-nya, bahkan kalau -ed-nya hilang (*We worked late last night*).

blocks.text: Practise with short clips (30 seconds is enough): listen once and write what you hear, then check with the subtitles. Look at what you missed: usually the small words and the dropped t's. Then play it again and speak along with the speaker, at the same speed (this is called **shadowing**).

id.text: Berlatihlah dengan klip pendek (30 detik sudah cukup): dengarkan sekali dan tulis apa yang kamu dengar, lalu cek dengan subtitle-nya. Lihat apa yang terlewat: biasanya kata-kata kecil dan t yang hilang. Lalu putar lagi dan ucapkan bersamaan dengan pembicaranya, dengan kecepatan yang sama (ini disebut **shadowing**).

blocks.prompt: Your friend asks quickly: 'Whatcha gonna do this weekend?' What are the full words?
options: What do you want to do this weekend?
What are you going to do this weekend?
What have you got to do this weekend?
blocks.explain: 'gonna' = *going to*, so the question is **What are you going to do this weekend?** ('whatcha' = *what are you*, said very fast). *want to* would be 'wanna' and *got to* would be 'gotta'.

id.prompt: Temanmu bertanya dengan cepat: 'Whatcha gonna do this weekend?' Apa kata-kata lengkapnya?
id.explain: 'gonna' = *going to*, jadi pertanyaannya **What are you going to do this weekend?** ('whatcha' = *what are you*, diucapkan sangat cepat). *want to* akan jadi 'wanna' dan *got to* akan jadi 'gotta'.

id.title: Mendengarkan bahasa Inggris yang cepat: kembalikan perubahannya

suggestedQuestions: Do I have to drop sounds like native speakers do?

resources.title: Pronunciation: Elision of /t/
resources.note: A short video from Tim's Pronunciation Workshop: Tim shows how a t between two consonant sounds often disappears in everyday British speech, with sentences to repeat. The title uses a phonetic symbol: /t/ simply means the t sound.

id.note: Video pendek dari Tim's Pronunciation Workshop: Tim menunjukkan bagaimana t di antara dua bunyi konsonan sering hilang dalam ucapan sehari-hari bahasa Inggris British, dengan kalimat-kalimat untuk ditirukan. Judulnya memakai simbol fonetik: /t/ artinya bunyi t saja.

Artikel ini juga menyebut bentuk seperti shoulda dan oughta, yang di luar pelajaran ini.

id.intro: Kamu sudah bisa menyambung kata dan membuat kata-kata kecil tetap lemah. Sekarang kenalan dengan bahasa Inggris yang benar-benar cepat: bunyi yang hilang (last night → 'las night'), bunyi yang berubah (ten people → 'tem people'), kata-kata kecil yang menyusut hampir tak terdengar, serta gonna, wanna dan gotta. Tujuan utamanya adalah memahami ucapan cepat, dan tahu bentuk mana yang boleh diucapkan tapi tidak boleh ditulis.
suggestedQuestions: Apakah aku harus menghilangkan bunyi seperti penutur asli?
Bolehkah aku bilang gonna di wawancara kerja?
Bagaimana cara berlatih memahami bahasa Inggris yang cepat?

assessment.cnx-1: Di sebuah rapat, manajermu bilang: 'I'm gonna send the new prices to the client tomorrow.' Tulis kalimat yang sama dengan kata-kata lengkap, seperti yang akan kamu tulis di email.
assessment.cnx-2: Sari bilang tentang rekan kerjanya: 'She's gotta pick up her kids at five.' Tulis kalimatnya dengan kata-kata lengkap, dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.cnx-3: Dalam ucapan cepat, 'next door' sering terdengar seperti 'nex door'. Bunyi apa yang hilang? Tulis hurufnya.
assessment.cnx-4: Di kantor, Rina bertanya ke Budi dengan cepat: 'Couldja check this email for me?' 'couldja' itu singkatan dari dua kata apa? Tulis kedua kata itu dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.cnx-5: Budi bilang dengan cepat: 'I've got the concert tickets. I'll send 'em to you tonight.' 'em itu kata apa? Tulis kata lengkapnya dalam bahasa Inggris.
assessment.cnx-6: Dengarkan. Tulis kata kecil yang kamu dengar di antara 'leave' dan 'the airport'.
assessment.cnx-7: Rina sedang menulis email ke pemasok. Kalimat mana yang sebaiknya dia pakai? Tulis A, B atau C. A: I wanna ask about the price. B: I would like to ask about the price. C: I gotta ask about the price.
